paragraphs: Sequence tasks often require connecting information separated by many time steps. Recurrent neural networks can theoretically retain relevant information through feedback connections, but training them to use long-term memory is difficult in practice. This paper introduces the Clockwork RNN, an architectural modification that gives different parts of the network different schedules for processing a sequence.

The hidden layer is divided into modules, with each module computing only at its assigned clock rate. This lets the architecture process inputs at multiple temporal granularities instead of requiring every hidden unit to operate at the same pace. The paper reports that this design reduces the number of parameters relative to a simple RNN and makes network evaluation faster.

Preliminary experiments cover audio signal generation, spoken word classification on TIMIT, and online handwriting recognition. The Clockwork RNN outperforms both simple RNNs and LSTMs on the spoken word task, and simple RNNs on handwriting recognition. These findings support the usefulness of scheduled hidden modules on the tested tasks; they do not establish superiority across all sequence problems.
icml-2014-a-clockwork-rnn-97d92b25e2.tldr: Clockwork RNNs update hidden modules at different rates, reducing parameters and evaluation cost while improving performance on the tested sequence tasks.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming needs machinery for carrying out inference as a program executes. This paper addresses that systems problem by introducing probabilistic C, an intermediate representation that other probabilistic programming languages can target. The goal is to make inference compatible with established compilation and operating system infrastructure.

The approach uses standard facilities such as processes, process forking, mutexes, and shared memory to implement forward inference techniques. The abstract specifically identifies sequential Monte Carlo and particle Markov chain Monte Carlo. These facilities provide the execution and coordination mechanisms needed to support inference, allowing the implementation to draw on capabilities already available in ordinary programming environments.

The authors developed and tested probabilistic C, which can be compiled into machine code using standard compilers and linked with operating system libraries. They describe the resulting target as efficient, scalable, and portable. Its broader significance is architectural: probabilistic language implementations can share a compilation destination, while hardware and systems research can investigate ways to optimize the execution infrastructure beneath them.
icml-2014-a-compilation-target-for-proba.tldr: Probabilistic C provides a tested compilation target that implements probabilistic inference using standard compilers and operating system facilities.

paragraphs: A parameterized skill is a flexible behavior intended to handle tasks drawn from a distribution of reinforcement learning problems. Learning such a skill involves deciding not only how to improve behavior, but also which tasks to practice. This paper focuses on selecting training tasks that are expected to produce useful improvements in the skill.

The method builds a nonparametric Bayesian model of skill performance. It then derives analytical expressions for an acquisition criterion that identifies tasks maximizing expected improvement. Because skill performance changes during training, the authors also introduce a spatiotemporal kernel tailored to nonstationary performance models. This makes changes over training part of the task-selection machinery.

The approach does not depend on a particular policy or skill representation, and the authors state that its scaling is independent of task dimensionality. They evaluate it using simulated nonlinear catapult control over arbitrarily mountainous terrain. The contribution is therefore a general method for deciding what to practice next, supported by an evaluation in a challenging control setting.
icml-2014-active-learning-of-parameteriz.tldr: A Bayesian performance model selects training tasks that maximize expected improvement when learning flexible reinforcement learning skills.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo estimation can offer several unbiased estimators for the same quantity, leaving a practical question: which estimator should receive the next allocation of computation? This paper studies sequential selection among such alternatives, with the aim of minimizing the mean squared error of the final estimate formed from their outputs.

The authors reduce this allocation problem to a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem. This connection lets them use established strategies for learning which choices are effective while continuing to make choices. Their analysis shows that the resulting mean squared error approaches what could be achieved by choosing the best estimator retrospectively, after its quality is known.

The paper also extends the approach to estimators whose computational costs differ and may themselves be random. That extension matters because allocating computation must account for expense as well as estimation quality. The resulting adaptive Monte Carlo strategies are presented as providing stronger guarantees than previous approaches together with practical advantages. The comparison target remains the best available estimator in hindsight, rather than an unrestricted ideal estimator.
icml-2014-adaptive-monte-carlo-via-bandi.tldr: Bandit allocation strategies adaptively choose among unbiased Monte Carlo estimators, approaching the error of the best retrospective choice while accommodating unequal costs.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the beta diffusion tree, a probabilistic tree structure for organizing objects into overlapping subsets. Such a collection is called a feature allocation: an object can belong to several subsets instead of being assigned to just one cluster. The tree adds a hierarchical organization to these potentially overlapping memberships.

The construction represents objects as particles moving through a continuous space. Its key distinction from the related clustering trees discussed in the abstract is that a particle can have multiple copies. Those copies can move to different locations, allowing one object to contribute to multiple groups. The process produces a random number of groups, with overlap arising directly from its generative mechanism.

The authors use this structure to build a factor analysis model with hierarchically clustered factors and develop Markov chain Monte Carlo inference over the possible trees. They demonstrate the approach through missing-data experiments involving gene expression, international development, and intranational socioeconomic measurements. These experiments illustrate applications of the model without establishing a specific comparative performance advantage in the abstract.
icml-2014-beta-diffusion-trees-8604e9dc5.tldr: Beta diffusion trees model hierarchical, overlapping groups by allowing copies of object-representing particles to follow different paths.

paragraphs: This paper incorporates the internal morphological structure of words into a vector-based probabilistic language model. Instead of treating word representations as disconnected from the parts that compose a word, the method integrates compositional morphological representations. The aim is to make this information useful for both language modeling and machine translation.

The authors study the approach in log-bilinear language models. They factor the vocabulary to make the models efficient enough to run inside a machine translation decoder. This computational step matters because a useful language model must also be practical to evaluate during translation, particularly when the target language has a large vocabulary and rich morphology.

Evaluations across a range of languages examine both the representations themselves and their use in downstream translation. The learned representations perform well on word similarity tasks, and the models substantially reduce perplexity. For translation into morphologically rich languages, improvements reach up to 1.2 BLEU points over a system using back-off n-gram models. That figure is the largest reported improvement, rather than a uniform gain across languages.
icml-2014-compositional-morphology-for-w.tldr: Compositional morphological word representations improve language modeling and yield translation gains of up to 1.2 BLEU points in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Estimating a network among many variables can become difficult to compute and interpret. Module graphical lasso addresses this by exploiting modularity: variables are organized into tightly connected groups, and the model estimates relationships among those groups. It combines substantial dimensionality reduction with network estimation in a Gaussian graphical model.

The method iteratively learns which variables belong to each module, a latent variable representing each module, and the parameters of the graphical model over those latent variables. The resulting graph describes conditional independencies among modules. Learning these components together makes the grouping and network structure parts of one estimation procedure rather than unrelated outputs.

On synthetic data, the method outperforms standard graphical lasso and three alternatives that incorporate latent variables. On ovarian cancer gene expression data, it outperforms standard clustering methods in identifying functionally coherent gene groups and predicting patient survival time. The authors also report biological insights and possible new drug targets from the learned modules and dependencies. These targets are proposed possibilities, not experimentally established treatments.
icml-2014-efficient-dimensionality-reduc.tldr: Module graphical lasso jointly learns variable groups and their dependency network, improving reported synthetic and ovarian cancer data results.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Bayesian networks and neural networks with stochastic hidden units are often treated as separate model families. This paper shows that they can often be expressed as instances of one another. The connection comes from changing how latent variables are parameterized, specifically by switching between centered and differentiable non-centered forms.

This change of representation matters computationally. The authors show that the choice can substantially affect the efficiency of gradient-based posterior inference. The two forms are often complementary, and the paper clarifies when each is preferable and how to make inference robust. The result supports choosing a parameterization according to the inference problem rather than assuming one form is always better.

In the non-centered form, a simple Monte Carlo estimator of marginal likelihood can also be used to learn model parameters. The paper therefore connects model representation to both posterior inference and parameter learning. Experiments support its theoretical results. Its central contribution is the ability to move between useful formulations and exploit their different computational properties, with transformations described as available often rather than universally.
icml-2014-efficient-gradient-based-infer.tldr: Switching latent-variable parameterizations often connects Bayesian and stochastic neural networks and can improve gradient-based inference.

paragraphs: Learning graphical models with hidden variables can involve difficult optimization landscapes. Method-of-moments approaches offer consistent estimates while avoiding local-optimum problems, but their applicability has been restricted to particular model types. This paper combines moment information with a composite marginal likelihood objective to extend the range of models that can be estimated consistently.

The key step uses tensor factorization to uncover partial information about hidden variables. Within the model class studied, that information makes an otherwise nonconvex negative log-likelihood convex. The recovered information therefore does more than provide an initial guess: it changes the optimization problem in a way that supports the paper's estimation guarantees.

The resulting class includes directed and undirected graphical models, including graphs with loops and high treewidth. For models outside that class, the authors describe an extension that incorporates the partial information through posterior regularization. The consistency result applies to the supported class; the abstract presents the outside-class construction as an extension, without assigning it the same guarantee. The broader contribution is a bridge between moment-based recovery and likelihood-based estimation.
icml-2014-estimating-latent-variable-gra.tldr: Combining tensor-derived hidden-variable information with composite likelihood yields consistent estimation for a broader class of graphical models.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from incomplete observations. This paper addresses settings where the observations are noisy and their statistical behavior extends beyond exact entries or additive Gaussian noise. It also considers structural information beyond low rank, motivated by data such as counts, binary measurements, and skewed continuous values.

The framework models observed entries using exponential-family distributions and expresses matrix structure through a general regularizer. This creates a common formulation for different observation models and constraints, including block sparsity and combinations of low-rank and elementwise sparse structure. Both the distribution of the measurements and the organization of the underlying matrix become explicit parts of the estimation problem.

The authors propose a convex regularized M-estimator and provide a unified statistical analysis for this class of estimators. Simulated datasets corroborate the theoretical results. The contribution is a broader framework in which varied matrix completion problems can be formulated and analyzed together. Its scope is defined by the exponential-family observation setting and the structural constraints represented by the regularizer.
icml-2014-exponential-family-matrix-comp.tldr: A convex estimation framework extends matrix completion to exponential-family observations and structural constraints beyond low rank.

paragraphs: The densest k-subgraph problem asks which set of k vertices contains the most edges. This paper develops an algorithm that searches a low-dimensional space for good solutions. Its theoretical performance bounds depend on the graph spectrum, connecting the quality of the approximation to mathematical properties of the input graph.

One guarantee applies when some k-vertex subgraph contains a constant fraction of all edges in the graph. Under that condition, the algorithm achieves an approximation factor arbitrarily close to two in polynomial time. The authors also establish nearly linear running time under spectral assumptions they describe as holding for most application graphs. Both results retain their stated conditions.

The method is designed to support large-scale parallel computation. A MapReduce implementation is evaluated on real-world graphs containing up to billions of edges, demonstrating its ability to operate at that scale. In those experiments, it finds significantly denser subgraphs than the previous state of the art. The paper thus combines conditional approximation guarantees with empirical evidence of scalability and solution quality on massive graphs.
icml-2014-finding-dense-subgraphs-via-lo.tldr: A low-dimensional search finds dense subgraphs with spectrum-dependent guarantees and strong empirical results on graphs with billions of edges.

paragraphs: Part-of-speech tagging assigns grammatical categories to words. Standard learned word representations capture useful syntactic and semantic information, but often leave out the internal shape and morphology of a word. This paper addresses that omission by learning representations from characters and using them together with conventional word representations.

The proposed deep neural network brings information from inside words into the tagging model without relying on handcrafted features. This matters because morphology and word shape can provide useful grammatical evidence, especially in morphologically rich languages. Combining the two representations gives the tagger access to both whole-word information and information learned from character structure.

The authors report state-of-the-art tagging results for English and Portuguese in their evaluations. Accuracy reaches 97.32% on the English Penn Treebank WSJ corpus and 97.47% on the Portuguese Mac-Morpho corpus. For Portuguese, the result corresponds to a 12.2% reduction in error relative to the best previously known result. These findings demonstrate the practical value of incorporating learned character-level information into the tested tagging systems.
icml-2014-learning-character-level-repre.tldr: Combining learned character and word representations produces strong English and Portuguese part-of-speech taggers without handcrafted features.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to recover an unknown network from contagion outcomes when detailed infection times are unavailable. The learner sees an initial set of infected vertices and the final set reached by a stochastic spreading process. It must infer network structure from these starting and ending sets, without observing the timing of each intermediate infection.

The authors introduce models covering two ways of obtaining the initial infections: the learner may actively choose them or passively observe them. This distinction separates settings where experiments can be designed from those where the available contagion events are simply recorded. In both cases, the information available is deliberately coarser than vertex-by-vertex timestamp histories.

The main theoretical results provide efficient, provably correct algorithms for exactly learning tree networks. The authors also give empirical evidence of good performance on realistic sparse graphs more generally. The distinction matters: exact recovery is theoretically established for trees, while the broader sparse-graph claim is experimental. The work shows that initial and final infection sets can retain enough information for rigorous network learning in the supported setting.
icml-2014-learning-from-contagion-withou.tldr: Initial and final contagion sets enable provably exact learning of tree networks, with encouraging empirical results on more general sparse graphs.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations whose dimensions have an order of importance. Its training procedure, nested dropout, randomly removes coherent nested sets of hidden units. The objective is to make the arrangement of information within a learned code useful, rather than treating all representation dimensions as interchangeable.

For a semi-linear autoencoder, the authors prove that nested dropout makes the units identifiable and leads to an exact equivalence with principal component analysis. They then extend the procedure to deep models. The exact PCA connection belongs to the analyzed semi-linear setting, while the deep-model extension supports a broader set of applications.

The ordered codes enable hash-based retrieval structures with lookup time logarithmic in database size and independent of representation dimensionality. The authors report using codes hundreds of times longer than previously feasible for retrieval, avoiding the quality loss associated with short codes while retaining competitive retrieval speed. They also show that ordered representations are promising for adaptive compression and efficient online reconstruction. Across these applications, ordering makes representation length a more usable computational choice.
icml-2014-learning-ordered-representatio.tldr: Nested dropout orders representation dimensions by importance, enabling long-code retrieval and promising adaptive compression.

paragraphs: A neural network's ability to represent a function does not by itself establish that gradient descent can learn it. This paper studies that distinction for low-degree polynomials. It focuses on networks with one hidden layer and a linear output, seeking theoretical conditions under which optimization succeeds despite the possibility of local minima.

The first result shows that gradient descent can learn any low-degree polynomial from a randomly initialized network with sufficiently many hidden units. A second result concerns complex-valued weights, even when the desired output function is real. Under suitable conditions, these networks have no robust local minima: random perturbations allow escape from a local minimum. The authors state that this property does not hold for real-valued weights.

The paper also discusses whether sparse polynomials can be learned using small networks whose size depends on the target's sparsity. That discussion is distinct from the stated guarantees for sufficiently wide networks and suitable complex-weight settings. Together, the results give conditional theoretical support for neural-network learning, while showing why network size and the choice of weight domain matter.
icml-2014-learning-polynomials-with-neur.tldr: The paper establishes conditional guarantees for learning low-degree polynomials and escaping local minima in certain complex-weight neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic model for learning representations organized around transformations of data. It targets compact commutative Lie groups, a class that includes image rotations and cyclic translations. The model produces invariant, equivariant, and disentangled representations, connecting how data change under transformations with how their representations are structured.

The authors define disentangling using a symmetry-based principle borrowed from physics, where a system's elementary components are understood through its symmetries. A newly identified Bayesian conjugacy relation makes probabilistic inference fully tractable over the supported group class. That tractability is central: the model can reason probabilistically about these transformations without leaving the mathematical setting in which inference is manageable.

Training uses pairs of image patches related by transformations. The authors show that the learned invariant representation is highly effective for classification. This gives an application-level result for the symmetry-based construction: a representation designed to remain stable under the modeled transformations can also be useful for recognizing classes. The tractability claim is specifically tied to compact commutative Lie groups, rather than arbitrary transformation families.
icml-2014-learning-the-irreducible-repre.tldr: A tractable probabilistic model of compact commutative Lie groups learns symmetry-based representations that are effective for image-patch classification.

paragraphs: This paper constructs a prediction-market model in which individually motivated trading has a shared mathematical interpretation. Agents are modeled using risk measures, and a market maker specifies the trading process. These modeling choices let the authors connect the behavior of the whole market to a global objective, even though each agent pursues its own goal.

The authors show that the market approaches this global objective and that its trading dynamics provide a sensible algorithm for optimizing it. The important connection is between local decisions and collective optimization: a sequence of trades can be studied as the operation of an optimization procedure. The result concerns the proposed model and its particular formulation of agents and trading.

This connection opens two directions of use. Machine learning methods can help analyze a market through its global objective. Conversely, certain machine learning problems can be approached by constructing and running a corresponding market. The paper therefore supplies a framework for translating between market dynamics and optimization, rather than assuming that arbitrary markets automatically solve arbitrary learning problems.
icml-2014-multi-period-trading-predictio.tldr: A risk-based prediction-market model connects self-interested trading to optimization of a global objective and certain machine learning problems.

paragraphs: Expressive directed models with hidden variables can be difficult to train because exact inference is intractable. This paper introduces a feedforward inference network that quickly produces samples from a variational posterior. Sampling is exact for that approximate posterior distribution; it does not make inference in the original model exact.

The inference network and the underlying model are trained jointly by maximizing a variational lower bound on log-likelihood. This supplies a shared training objective while avoiding an iterative inference procedure for each input. A naive gradient estimator for the inference network has impractically high variance, so the authors apply several model-independent variance reduction techniques to make training useful.

The approach is applied to sigmoid belief networks and deep autoregressive networks. In the reported evaluations, it outperforms wake-sleep on MNIST and achieves state-of-the-art results on the Reuters RCV1 document dataset. These findings support the combination of a learned feedforward approximation and variance-controlled training as a practical route to fitting expressive latent-variable models on larger datasets.
icml-2014-neural-variational-inference-a.tldr: A jointly trained feedforward inference network makes variational learning practical through fast sampling and model-independent gradient variance reduction.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning uses information about which data pairs should be close and which should be separated. The paper argues that conventional objectives based on covariance matrices are vulnerable to outlying samples and features because they sum squared L2 distances. It proposes an objective based on L1 distances to make metric learning more robust.

The new objective creates its own optimization challenge. It simultaneously minimizes and maximizes multiple nonsmooth L1 terms, reflecting the different roles of must-link and cannot-link constraints. The authors systematically derive an efficient iterative algorithm for this general L1 minmax problem. This solver is a theoretical contribution in addition to its use in the proposed distance-learning method.

Empirical evaluations compare the method with related state-of-the-art approaches across several clustering settings. The proposed method performs better in the reported experiments on both noiseless and noisy data. These results support the practical value of the L1 formulation, while the algorithm addresses the computational difficulty introduced by optimizing attraction and separation terms together.
icml-2014-robust-distance-metric-learnin.tldr: An L1-based distance-learning objective and iterative minmax solver improve clustering results in the paper's noisy and noiseless evaluations.

paragraphs: Finding a linear binary classifier also raises a complementary question: what can an algorithm return when the classification constraints cannot be satisfied? This paper treats classifier construction and approximate certification of infeasibility within one process. It does so by connecting both tasks to a bilinear saddle point problem.

The authors show that the accelerated primal-dual method Mirror Prox can return either a linear classifier or an ε-infeasibility certificate. They establish convergence rates of O(√log n / ρ(A)) for the classifier case and O(√log n / ε) for the certificate case. These rates have only a weak dependence on problem size n, although the other quantities still affect convergence.

The framework also handles kernelized and conic versions with the same convergence rates. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings and highlight efficiency and numerical stability, especially for large instances. The contribution is a unified optimization perspective that provides a useful outcome on either side of feasibility, with the certificate explicitly expressed at an ε level of approximation.
icml-2014-saddle-points-and-accelerated-.tldr: A saddle-point formulation uses Mirror Prox to find a linear classifier or an approximate infeasibility certificate with weak problem-size dependence.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to apply derivative-based regularization to functions that are linear in their parameters. Such penalties constrain a function through its derivatives, making the behavior of the function part of the learning objective. The proposed method, sample-based approximate regularization, offers a way to approximate these penalties using sampled information.

The construction combines sampling with finite-difference approximations of the relevant derivatives. Finite differences use changes in function values to approximate derivative information, while sampling supplies the information used to build the approximate regularizer. The method targets general derivative-based penalties within the stated class of linearly parameterized functions, rather than a single named penalty.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees comparing the approximate regularizers with the original ones and prove efficient convergence of the approximations. This comparison matters because computationally approximating a penalty should preserve its intended effect closely enough to remain meaningful. They also examine empirical performance on several datasets. The abstract establishes approximation fidelity and convergence as the main theoretical findings, alongside that empirical investigation.
icml-2014-sample-based-approximate-regul.tldr: Sample-based approximate regularization combines sampling and finite differences to approximate derivative penalties with fidelity and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Multiway tensors organize data along several dimensions, and many applications observe only a small fraction of their entries. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for low-rank decomposition of such incomplete data. A multiplicative gamma process prior sidesteps the need to specify the decomposition rank in advance.

The framework handles continuous and binary observations through conjugate Bayesian analysis. For binary data, where conjugacy is not directly available, Pólya-Gamma sampling enables closed-form Gibbs updates. The resulting samplers have time complexity linear in the number of observed tensor entries. This makes the approach particularly attractive when the full tensor is enormous but only a small number of entries are known.

The method can also be extended to supervised settings where entities along one or more tensor dimensions have labels. On synthetic and benchmark real-world datasets, the authors report better performance than several state-of-the-art tensor decomposition methods. The contribution combines flexibility about rank and observation type with computation that scales according to observed data, supported by the reported comparative experiments.
icml-2014-scalable-bayesian-low-rank-dec.tldr: A Bayesian tensor decomposition framework avoids fixing rank beforehand and supports continuous or binary data with computation linear in observed entries.

paragraphs: Bayesian time series models can represent complex sequential data, but inference becomes challenging on large datasets. Stochastic variational inference offers a way to approximate posterior distributions with only a small number of passes through the data. This paper develops that approach for several established families of Bayesian time series models.

The supported models include hidden Markov models, hidden semi-Markov models, and their nonparametric HDP variants. Developing inference algorithms for these families extends the scalable variational framework to models built around temporal structure. The contribution is therefore an adaptation of posterior approximation machinery to a collection of sequential modeling settings.

The authors also address a remaining computational bottleneck: hidden semi-Markov inference can be expensive even when performed on minibatches. They introduce fast approximate updates for duration distributions that are negative binomial or mixtures of negative binomials. These updates give an additional computational mechanism for those specified duration models. The paper's stated contribution is the inference algorithms and targeted approximations, rather than a reported numerical improvement on a particular benchmark.
icml-2014-stochastic-variational-inferen.tldr: The paper develops stochastic variational inference for Bayesian time series models, including faster approximate semi-Markov updates for specified duration distributions.

paragraphs: This paper presents a speech recognition system that maps audio directly to text without requiring an intermediate phonetic representation. It combines a deep bidirectional LSTM recurrent network with the Connectionist Temporal Classification objective. The approach places direct transcription at the center of the recognition system.

The authors modify the training objective to minimize the expected value of an arbitrary transcription loss. This allows training to target word error rate directly, including when no lexicon or language model is available. The change matters because it connects optimization to errors in the resulting transcription, rather than relying only on the original objective.

On the Wall Street Journal corpus, the system achieves 27.3% word error rate without prior linguistic information. Adding only a lexicon gives 21.9%, while using a trigram language model gives 8.2%. Combining the network with a baseline system reduces the rate further to 6.7%. These results demonstrate direct audio-to-text recognition while also showing the substantial benefits of linguistic resources and system combination in the reported setting.
icml-2014-towards-end-to-end-speech-reco.tldr: A deep bidirectional LSTM transcribes audio directly into text, with modified training that can optimize word error rate without a lexicon or language model.

paragraphs: Many matrix completion guarantees assume that observed entries are sampled uniformly at random and sampled anew for each matrix. This paper studies a more reusable guarantee: when can one sampling pattern support exact recovery across a class of low-rank matrices? It allows a variety of sampling schemes rather than relying solely on fresh random observations.

The authors represent observed positions as edges of a bipartite graph. If that graph has a sufficiently large spectral gap, nuclear norm minimization exactly recovers all low-rank matrices satisfying the stated incoherence properties. Universality therefore concerns recovery across an eligible matrix class using a suitable observation pattern; it does not remove the conditions on the graph or matrices.

Under stricter incoherence conditions, the paper also shows that O(nr²) uniformly sampled entries suffice to recover any eligible rank-r, n-by-n matrix. This contrasts with O(nr log n) bounds in other algorithms and existing analyses. The comparison changes both rank dependence and the assumptions, so it is not an unconditional sample-efficiency improvement for every rank.
icml-2014-universal-matrix-completion-1a.tldr: Suitable sampling graphs permit universal low-rank matrix recovery by nuclear norm minimization under specified incoherence conditions.
